name: Yameo
confidence_why: The only statement on Yameo stress is Peña's 2009 second-hand summary of Espinosa 1955, which says each word carries one accented, lengthened syllable but gives no placement rule and treats the accent as stress rather than tone only for lack of evidence, while Rivet 1911, Loukotka 1968 and Wise 1999 say nothing about stress.

catalog_quote: [p. 152] Espinoza (1955:293) states that in Yameo the pronunciation of vowels in unaccented final syllables is shortened, thus the vowel is short. Therefore, the vowels in the other syllables are perceived as long, he concludes. Further, Espinoza says that he is marking the stress syllable with an accent, indicating both that it carries the stress of the word and that the vowel is 'longer' than the ones in other syllables (294). [p. 153] ... while Espinoza describes Yameo as having long vowels in just the stressed syllable. [p. 103] Because of lack of evidence, an accent mark in Yameo is interpreted as just marking stress. [p. 20 fn. 13] In later chapters, especially for Yameo, an accent means that the vowel is stressed but it does not necessarily indicates tone since tone is not represented in the Peba or Yameo sources used for this thesis.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible statement is second-hand: Espinosa (1955) recorded Yameo word stress lexically, writing an acute on the stressed syllable of each word, and noted that the stressed vowel is lengthened while vowels of unstressed final syllables are shortened. Neither Espinosa-as-reported nor Peña gives a rule for which syllable carries stress, so the position of stress cannot be classified from what is accessible.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Peña adds that Espinosa's 'long' (stressed) vowels mostly do not correspond to Yagua long vowels and that Espinosa's transcription is hyper-phonetic and inconsistent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in Espinosa's citation forms (elicited c. 1950 from the last elderly speakers at San Regis); Peña explicitly treats Espinosa's accent marks as stress, not tone, 'because of lack of evidence'.
new_statements.identity_note: Peña's Yameo data are Espinosa's San Regis (San Francisco de Regis) variety recorded c. 1950 plus Tessmann 1930; the 18th-century 'Yameo-Masamae' doctrina texts (Masamae = Mazán variety, treated by Loukotka as a Yameo dialect) carry no prosodic information. All fall under yame1242; Glottolog has no separate dialect codes.

sources.note: Second-hand only (pp. 20 fn.13, 103, 152-153): Espinosa (1955:293-294) marks the stressed syllable of each Yameo word with an accent; vowels of unaccented final syllables are shortened, stressed vowels 'longer'; Peña interprets Espinosa's accent marks as stress (not tone). No rule for the position of stress is reported.
No stress statement; phonology tables derive from Peña 2009. fr-wiki reproduces Loukotka 1968 Yameo forms with acute accents (wi-náto 'head', natéra 'sun', pwitér 'one', narámue 'two') but no rule.
